record.original_question: Given two polytopes P and Q, when does there exist a polytope whose facets are each isomorphic to either P or Q, and when can such a polytope be finite?

evidence.quote: Problem 19. Given two polytopes P and Q, when is there a polytope whose facets are each isomorphic to P or Q? When is there a finite such polytope?

artifact.self_contained_problem:
An abstract polytope of rank $n$ is a partially ordered set $(\mathcal{P},\le)$ with a least face $F_{-1}$ and a greatest face $F_n$, such that every maximal chain (flag) has length $n+2$, $\mathcal{P}$ is strongly flag-connected, and the diamond condition holds: whenever $F<G$ with $\mathrm{rank}(G)-\mathrm{rank}(F)=2$, there are exactly two faces $H$ with $F<H<G$. The faces of rank $n-1$ are called the facets of $\mathcal{P}$, and each facet, regarded with the induced order, is itself an abstract polytope of rank $n-1$.

Let $P$ and $Q$ be two abstract polytopes of the same rank $n-1$ (with $P\not\cong Q$). 

(a) Determine necessary and sufficient conditions on the pair $(P,Q)$ for the existence of an abstract polytope $\mathcal{R}$ of rank $n$ such that every facet of $\mathcal{R}$ is isomorphic to either $P$ or to $Q$, and both isomorphism types occur among the facets of $\mathcal{R}$.

(b) Determine necessary and sufficient conditions on $(P,Q)$ for the existence of such an $\mathcal{R}$ that is moreover finite (i.e., has finitely many faces).
artifact.status_search_result: The question of characterizing pairs $(P,Q)$ of abstract polytopes that can serve as the two facet isomorphism types of a (finite) abstract polytope is a recognized open problem in the theory of abstract polytopes. While the regular case (all facets isomorphic) is well studied, no general characterization for the two-facet-type or finite two-facet-type cases is known, and the search did not surface any solution.

status_evidence.title: Abstract polytope - Wikipedia
status_evidence.snippet: Any regular abstract polytope has isomorphic regular (n−1)-faces and isomorphic regular vertex figures... weaker concepts, some not yet fully standardized, such as semi-regular, quasi-regular, uniform, chiral, and Archimedean apply to polytopes that have some, but not all of their faces equivalent in each rank.
status_evidence.claim: General mixed-facet-type characterizations are not standardized; the question of which pairs of facet types can be realized remains a research problem.
